growth_story.headline: Turkmenistan's gas-fed, state-led boom gave way to slower growth after 2015, and the official figures that show steady gains are hard to check.
growth_story.arc: In 1990-1997 income per person shrank by 3.6 percent a year: after the Soviet Union ended, Turkmenistan's gas could flow only to former Soviet buyers, those buyers ran up unpaid bills, and supply was halted between 1997 and 1999. Growth returned at 4.9 percent a year in 1998-2005, though outside observers found the national accounts of that time very opaque. The boom came in 2006-2014 at 8.7 percent a year, built on gas, state-led investment and new gas exports to China, with investment rising from 18.6 percent of GDP in 2007 to 48.3 percent in 2012. In 2015 gas prices fell, a dispute with Russia's Gazprom cut export earnings and the manat was devalued, and growth slowed to 4.1 percent a year in 2015-2025. Over 2016-2025 it averaged 4.1 percent a year, against 8.2 in the decade before. On the official numbers, income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, while investment has fallen back to 16.5 percent of GDP.

threads.title: Gas sold to one market
threads.text: Growth still rests on natural gas, and its exports go mainly to one market, China. That ties output to China's demand. It also ties output to the few transit routes out of a landlocked country.

since_last_year.text: The two main lenders now tell different stories. In June 2026, IMF staff said the official growth figures are hard to square with other data, used their own estimates instead, reported that the hydrocarbon sector shrank again in 2025, and expected growth to slow in 2026. In October 2026, the World Bank reported strong official growth in the first half of 2026 and expected it to stay strong, helped by a new phase of the Galkynysh gas field launched in April 2026.

growth_story.tension: The data follow official figures, which show income per person growing between 3.6 and 4.6 percent every year from 2015 to 2025, even through the 2020 pandemic and swings in gas prices. IMF staff find the official growth story hard to square with other data, use their own estimates, and report that the hydrocarbon sector shrank in 2024 and 2025. The World Bank and the EBRD also point to limited or unreliable official data. So the steady era since 2015, and the 2025 peak, may overstate what happened. Doubts about Turkmenistan's accounts go back to the 1990s.
